mainTopic: Rented donkeys that get sick or die on the way, רב's rule against using up the principal, and a rented boat that sinks
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about a rented donkey that is taken away, and names רבי שמעון בן אלעזר as its author. The גמרא asks how that fits another ruling of his about a sick donkey. It answers that renting a donkey for riding, or for carrying glass, is different. Next, רב rules that if a riding donkey dies halfway, the renter pays for half the trip and has only a complaint. The גמרא works out the exact case: no donkeys are available, a specific donkey was promised, and its body is worth too little to buy another. It explains that רב holds the principal may not be used up (לא מכלינן קרנא), so the money cannot be spent on renting. That rule is the subject of a dispute with שמואל, who allows it. A ברייתא about a pledged tree that dried up seems to challenge רב, and the גמרא answers in several ways, involving sixty-year sales and יובל. Finally, a new ברייתא brings רבי נתן's ruling on a rented boat that sank halfway, and the גמרא begins testing what kind of deal it means.

steps.title: The ברייתא's ruling on a seized donkey belongs to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by naming רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. He rules that if the seized donkey is taken along the renter's route, the owner can say 'here is yours.' If not, the owner must provide another donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the words of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. He used to say: if the donkey was seized and taken in the direction it was already going, the owner can tell the renter, 'Your donkey is right in front of you.' If not, the owner must give him another donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא and tells us whose opinion it is: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר draws a line based on where the seized donkey is taken. If it goes the same way the renter was traveling, the renter has not really lost his ride, so the owner is free of responsibility. If it is taken somewhere else, the owner must replace it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The words of': names who holds this opinion
In the direction it was walking
'Here, yours is in front of you': the owner has no further obligation
He must supply him with a donkey

phrases.english: These are the words of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: For Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would say:
If it was seized and taken along the way it was going,
the owner says to him: Yours is before you,
and if not,
he is obligated to provide him with a donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted just before this section and gives the name of its author.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seized donkey taken along the renter's route frees the owner; otherwise he must provide a replacement donkey.

steps.title: Challenge: the first part of the ברייתא contradicts רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the whole ברייתא can follow רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. Its first part says a sick or crazed donkey frees the owner. Elsewhere, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the owner must replace such a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really say this ברייתא follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר? Its first part teaches that if a rented donkey got sick or went mad, the owner can say, 'Yours is in front of you.' But רבי שמעון בן אלעזר said that if someone rented a donkey to ride, and it got sick or went mad, the owner must provide another donkey!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that the ברייתא is רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's. It points to another ruling of his that seems to clash with the ברייתא's opening clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening of the ברייתא lets the owner off the hook when the donkey gets sick or goes mad. A different teaching of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר makes the owner replace a sick or mad donkey. If one person said both, they seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you really establish it (as following this opinion)?
The first clause of the teaching

steps.confusionAlert: Look closely at the two rulings. The ברייתא just says 'one who rents a donkey,' but רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ruling says 'to ride on it.' That small difference is exactly what the answer will use.

phrases.english: And can you establish it
phrases.notes: 'It' is the whole ברייתא, including its first part.

phrases.english: in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?
But the first clause teaches:
One who rents the donkey
and it became sick or went mad,
the owner says to him: Yours is before you.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר:
phrases.english: Whereas Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said:
One who rents the donkey to ride on it
and it became sick or went mad,
the owner is obligated to provide him with a donkey!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי מָצֵית מוֹקְמַתְּ לַהּ כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר? וְהָא קָתָנֵי רֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks Step 1's claim that the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the whole ברייתא, including its first clause, follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause frees the owner when the donkey becomes sick or mad. Another ruling of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר obligates him in that same situation, so both cannot be his.

steps.title: Answer: renting a donkey for riding is a different case
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא answers that riding is different. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ruling is only about a riding donkey, while the ברייתא's first clause is about a donkey rented for other work.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: Renting a donkey to ride on it is different.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא resolves the contradiction by splitting the two rulings into two different kinds of rental.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A rider needs a donkey that walks steadily, so a sick or crazed donkey is useless to him, and the owner must replace it. When a donkey is rented to carry ordinary loads, a sick donkey can still do the job, so the owner can say 'here is yours.' Now both rulings can belong to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatToRemember: Riding is the exception. A sick donkey rented for riding must be replaced, but a sick donkey rented for carrying loads need not be.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
Renting to ride on it is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: riding versus carrying loads.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rulings deal with the same kind of rental, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ruling is only about riding. The ברייתא's first clause is about other uses, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: Carrying glass vessels counts like riding
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא adds that renting a donkey to carry glass vessels is treated like renting it for riding.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Glass vessels are treated like riding on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא builds on רבה בר רב הונא's answer and adds one more case that belongs in the 'riding' group.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Glass breaks easily, so a donkey carrying it must walk steadily, just like one carrying a rider. That means a sick or crazed donkey is useless for this job too, and the owner must provide another one.

keyTerms.meaning: Is similar to, is treated like

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
And glass vessels
are like riding on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends Step 3's 'riding is different' rule to another case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A donkey rented to carry glass vessels is judged like a donkey rented for riding.

steps.title: A riding donkey that dies halfway through the trip
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא quotes רב: if a donkey rented for riding dies halfway, the renter pays for half the trip. The renter can complain about the trouble, but he has no legal claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said in the name of רב: If someone rents a donkey to ride, and it dies halfway through the trip, he pays the owner for half the trip. He can only complain against the owner; he has no legal claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new statement of רב about a rented riding donkey that dies in the middle of the journey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter pays only for the part of the trip he actually used. He is now stuck partway and must find another donkey, which is a real hardship. Still, all he has is a grievance, meaning he can be upset with the owner, but he cannot demand money or a replacement in court.

keyTerms.meaning: A grievance or complaint, with no legal claim behind it

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with Step 2's case of a sick donkey. Here the donkey died, and רב says the renter has no legal claim, only a complaint.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said that Rav said:
One who rents the donkey to ride on it
and it died on him halfway through the journey,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתֵן לוֹ שְׂכָרוֹ שֶׁל חֲצִי הַדֶּרֶךְ,
phrases.english: gives him his fee for half the journey,
and he has nothing against him but a grievance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about a riding donkey that dies partway through the trip.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a riding donkey dies halfway, the renter pays for half the trip and has only a grievance, not a legal claim, against the owner.

steps.title: Why would the renter complain, and why would he pay?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests both possible settings of רב's case. Neither seems to fit both parts of the ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If donkeys are easy to rent there, why does he have a complaint at all? If donkeys are not available to rent, why should he have to pay the owner?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling from Step 5 by asking what the setting is. It shows that each possible setting seems to break one half of the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said two things: the renter pays for half the trip, and he has a complaint (תרעומת). If donkeys are easy to rent, he loses nothing, so there is nothing to complain about. If donkeys are not available, the donkey failed at the job, so why should he pay at all?

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What exactly is the case?
A complaint or grievance, with no legal claim behind it

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If donkeys are available for rent,
what is the complaint doing here?
If donkeys are not available for rent,
should he have to give him a fee?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling in Step 5 by testing which setting it could describe.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the renter pays for half and has only תרעומת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided dilemma: if donkeys are available, there is no basis for a complaint; if they are not, there is no basis for payment.

steps.title: No donkeys available, but he still pays for the distance traveled
steps.stepSummary: The case is where no donkeys are available. He still pays, because the owner can say: you would have paid to get this far anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is where donkeys are not available to rent. He pays because the owner can tell him: if you had wanted to travel just this far, wouldn't you have had to pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is where no other donkeys can be rented. It explains why the renter must still pay for half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The complaint makes sense because he is now stuck with no donkey. The payment also makes sense, because the donkey really did carry him halfway, and that part of the trip has value. So both halves of רב's ruling fit this setting.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (introduces the answer that keeps one side of the question)

phrases.english: Actually, it is where donkeys are not available for rent,
and he pays because the owner can say to him:
If you had wanted to come only up to here,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the spot where the donkey died, halfway along the road.

phrases.english: wouldn't you have had to pay a fee?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 6 by choosing the 'not available' side and justifying the payment.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case and giving a reason for the payment
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If no donkeys are available, the renter should owe nothing, since the job failed.
steps.terutzMaskana: He owes for the distance he was carried, because traveling that far has its own value. His being stranded is what gives him a complaint.

steps.title: What kind of donkey was promised?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the owner promised 'a donkey' or 'this donkey.' Either way, רב's ruling seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the owner said 'a donkey' in general, he has to give him another donkey. If he said 'this donkey,' then if its value is enough to buy another one, he should buy one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second question about רב's case, this time about what exactly was rented. It shows that each option seems to give a different result from רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no specific donkey was promised, the owner still owes a donkey, so the renter should get a replacement, not pay half. If a specific donkey was promised, the renter can sell the dead body and buy another donkey to finish the trip. Either way, the renter should not be left with only a complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A donkey' in general, with no specific animal named
Its value (here, the money from the dead donkey)

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If he said to him: 'a donkey,' with none specified,

phrases.aramaic: הָא חַיָּיב לְהַעֲמִיד לוֹ חֲמוֹר אַחֵר.
phrases.english: then he is obligated to provide him with another donkey.
If he said to him: 'this donkey,'
if its value is enough to buy one, let him buy one!
phrases.notes: 'Its value' is the money from selling the dead donkey's body.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״חֲמוֹר סְתָם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling where the case happens, the גמרא now asks what kind of rental agreement it involves.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the renter is left paying half with only a complaint
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With an unspecified donkey, the owner must replace it. With a specific donkey, the renter can buy a new one from the body's value. Neither leaves the renter stuck.

steps.title: The dead donkey is not worth enough to buy another
steps.stepSummary: רב's ruling is about 'this donkey,' where the body's value is too little to buy a new donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where its value is not enough to buy another donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is 'this donkey,' and the dead body is not worth enough to buy a replacement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a specific donkey, the owner does not have to replace it. If the body cannot pay for a new donkey, the renter really is stuck. That is why he pays half and has only a complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (this narrower case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed only
where its value is not enough to buy another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by narrowing the case to 'this donkey' with too little value to buy a new one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The renter can always replace the donkey, so רב's case could not happen.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a specific donkey whose body is worth too little to buy another.

steps.title: Then let him rent a donkey with the money
steps.stepSummary: Even if the body cannot buy a new donkey, the money could pay to rent one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If its value is enough to rent a donkey, let him rent one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer in Step 9. If the money can at least rent a donkey for the rest of the trip, the renter is not stuck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Renting costs much less than buying. So even a small amount of money from the body should get the renter to his destination, and he should have nothing to complain about.

phrases.english: If its value is enough to rent one, let him rent one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 9 by suggesting renting instead of buying.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the body cannot buy a new donkey
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Renting is cheaper, so the money could rent a donkey, and the renter would still not be stuck.

steps.title: רב's rule: we do not use up the principal
steps.stepSummary: רב follows his own view that the principal may not be used up. The body's value may not be spent on rental.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב follows his usual reasoning, because רב said: we do not use up the principal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב holds the money from the dead donkey cannot be spent on rental fees. Doing that would wipe out the owner's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buying a new donkey keeps the value: the money just turns into another donkey. Renting spends the money, and nothing is left for the owner. רב does not allow using up the principal (קרנא), so the renter cannot rent, and he is left with only a complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: We use up, we spend completely
The principal, the base value of the property

steps.whatToRemember: רב's case: a specific donkey ('this donkey') dies halfway, no donkeys are available, and its body cannot buy a new one. The renter pays for the distance he traveled. He cannot spend the body's value on rental, because רב holds לא מכלינן קרנא. So all he has left is a complaint.
steps.whyThisMatters: It ties this ruling to a broader rule of רב: the principal must be kept, not used up. This shapes how money from a lost or damaged rented item may be used.

phrases.english: Rav follows his own reasoning,
as Rav said:
We do not use up the principal.
phrases.notes: Buying another donkey keeps the value. Renting spends it, and then nothing is left for the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב לְטַעְמֵיהּ, דְּאָמַר רַב: לָא מְכַלֵּינַן קַרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by pointing to רב's general rule against using up the principal.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to the speaker's known general view (לטעמיה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The renter could just spend the body's value on renting a donkey.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב forbids using up the principal, so the money may not be spent on rental.

steps.title: The source for רב's view: the donkey that died halfway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the dispute between רב and שמואל. רב says the money from the dead donkey may buy a new donkey but may not pay to rent one. שמואל says it may even be used to rent one.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: Someone rented a donkey and it died halfway through the trip. רב said: If the value of its body is enough to buy a donkey, he should buy one. If it is only enough to rent one, he should not rent. שמואל said: Even if it is only enough to rent, he may rent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where we know רב's view from, the view it used in step 11. It quotes a dispute between רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said רב follows his own view. Here is that view. When a rented donkey dies, its body still has some value. רב allows that value to buy a new donkey, because the owner still ends up with something. He does not allow it to be spent on rent, because then nothing is left. שמואל allows renting too.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was stated (introduces an earlier statement of אמוראים)
With its value (the money from selling the dead donkey's body)

phrases.english: As it was stated: One who rents a donkey
and it died on him halfway through the journey.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: אִם יֵשׁ בְּדָמֶיהָ לִיקַּח – יִקַּח,
phrases.english: Rav said: If there is enough in its value to buy, he should buy,
but if only enough to rent, he should not rent.
And Shmuel said: Even if only enough to rent, he may rent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the claim in step 11 that רב follows his own view.
steps.raayaObject: That רב holds the principal may not be used up.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The dispute of רב and שמואל about a rented donkey that died halfway through the journey.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle רב and שמואל are arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the argument. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know what each one rules, but not why. The גמרא wants the one principle that splits them.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the dispute quoted in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides רב and שמואל.

steps.title: May the principal be used up?
steps.stepSummary: רב holds we do not use up the principal. שמואל holds we do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב holds: We do not use up the principal. שמואל holds: We do use up the principal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The argument is about whether you may use up the principal, which here means the value of the donkey's body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buying a new donkey keeps the value alive, so רב allows it. Renting spends the money, and nothing is left for the owner. That is "using up the principal," which רב forbids and שמואל allows.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: לא מכלינן קרנא, so the base value may not be spent away. שמואל: מכלינן קרנא, so it may.

phrases.english: Rav holds: We do not use up the principal.
And Shmuel holds: We do use up the principal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether the principal may be used up. רב says no, שמואל says yes.

steps.title: Challenge from the dried-up tree
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if a tree dried up, land is bought with its value. But land goes back to its owner at יובל, so the principal is used up. That seems to go against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If the tree dried up or was cut down, both are forbidden to use it. What should be done? Land should be bought with it, and he eats the produce. But here, when יובל comes, the land goes back to its owner, and the principal is used up!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's rule from a ברייתא. In the ברייתא, buying land is allowed even though the value seems to disappear in the end.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's fix for the tree is to buy land and eat its produce. But bought land returns to its original owner at יובל. So in the end the value is gone, which is "using up the principal." רב says that is forbidden, so the ברייתא seems to contradict him.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged (introduces a challenge from a ברייתא)
The Jubilee year, when sold fields return to their owners

phrases.english: They challenged: If the tree dried up or was cut down,
phrases.notes: This is a tree given as a pledge for a loan, so the lender may eat its fruit.

phrases.english: both are forbidden to use it.
What should be done?

phrases.aramaic: יִלָּקַח בּוֹ קַרְקַע, וְהוּא אוֹכֵל פֵּירוֹת.
phrases.english: Land should be bought with it, and he eats the produce.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא הָכָא, כֵּיוָן דְּכִי מָטֵי יוֹבֵל
phrases.english: But here, since when the Jubilee arrives
the land goes back to its owner,
and the principal is used up!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's principle from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that the principal may not be used up.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows buying land that returns at יובל. That uses up the principal, which רב forbids.

steps.title: The land was bought for sixty years
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about land bought for a fixed sixty years. That kind of sale does not return at יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where he bought it for sixty years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains the ברייתא as a case where the land was bought for sixty years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sale for a set number of years does not go back at יובל. So the land stays for the full time, and the principal is not suddenly lost. The ברייתא no longer goes against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (introduces a narrower case)

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
Where he bought it for sixty years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא spoke of a normal land purchase that returns at יובל, so the principal is used up.
steps.terutzMaskana: The land was bought for sixty years and does not return at יובל, so the principal is not used up.

steps.title: Proof that a sale for a fixed time does not return at יובל
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא in the name of רב קטינא learns from a פסוק that a field sold for sixty years does not return at יובל. Only a sale that would otherwise be forever is cut off by יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב חסדא said in the name of רב קטינא: From where do we know that one who sells his field for sixty years, it does not return at יובל? As it says: "And the land shall not be sold forever." A sale that would be forever if there were no יובל is not forever because there is יובל. That leaves out this sale, which is not forever even without יובל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer with a source. It shows from a פסוק that a fixed-time sale does not go back at יובל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says land may not be sold "forever." יובל only cancels a sale that would otherwise last forever. A sale for sixty years was never forever, so יובל does not touch it.
steps.whatToRemember: A field sold for a fixed number of years does not return at יובל. The next step asks whether this really saves רב's rule.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא:
phrases.english: As Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Ketina:
From where do we know that one who sells his field for sixty years,
it does not return at the Jubilee?
As it says: "And the land shall not be sold forever."
A sale that, if there were no Jubilee, would be forever,
since there is a Jubilee, is not forever.

phrases.aramaic: יָצְתָה זוֹ, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין שָׁם יוֹבֵל
phrases.english: This one is left out, since even if there were no Jubilee
it would not be forever.
phrases.notes: A sixty-year sale ends on its own anyway, so the פסוק about יובל doesn't apply to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 16 with a source.
steps.raayaObject: That a field sold for sixty years does not return at יובל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק "והארץ לא תמכר לצמיתות" as explained by רב חסדא in the name of רב קטינא.

steps.title: Even a sixty-year sale ends and the land goes back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 16. A sixty-year sale also ends, the land returns to its owner, and the principal is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, when the sixty years are over, the land goes back to its owner, and the principal is used up!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging the answer it just gave. Buying land for sixty years does not really solve the problem for רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 said a sixty-year sale does not return at יובל, so the value is kept. But the sixty years themselves eventually run out. Then the land goes back anyway, and the money from the tree is still lost, which goes against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: in the end; when all is said and done

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף סוֹף, לְכִי מָטוּ שִׁיתִּין שְׁנִין –
phrases.english: In the end, when sixty years arrive –
the land goes back to its owner,
and the principal is used up!
phrases.notes: The 'principal' here is the value of the dried-up tree that was used to buy the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: סוֹף סוֹף, לְכִי מָטוּ שִׁיתִּין שְׁנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the sixty-year answer that Steps 16-17 set up and proved.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 16, that the ברייתא means land bought for sixty years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A sixty-year sale still ends, so the land returns and the principal is used up. That is the very problem רב was trying to avoid.

steps.title: The ברייתא means a time when יובל is not in effect
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new answer. The ברייתא is talking about a time when יובל is not kept, so land can be bought forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what are we dealing with here? A time when יובל is not in effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the sixty-year answer and gives a new one. The ברייתא is talking about a time when the laws of יובל do not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When יובל is not in effect, land bought with the tree's value stays with the buyer forever. So the principal is never used up, and the ברייתא fits רב after all.

keyTerms.meaning: what case are we dealing with here?
at a time when the laws of יובל are not in effect

phrases.english: Rather, what are we dealing with here?
A time when יובל is not in effect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 18 by changing what case the ברייתא is about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): placing the ברייתא in a time when יובל is not kept.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be about land that goes back, so the principal would be used up.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a time without יובל, when the land is kept forever. It fits רב.

steps.title: Support: otherwise just chop the tree for firewood
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the new answer. If the principal could be used up, there would be no reason to buy land; the lender could simply take the tree as firewood.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you thought it was a time when יובל is in effect and we do use up the principal, let him just chop the tree into firewood and take it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings logical support for the answer in Step 19. The ברייתא's own ruling shows it must be talking about a time without יובל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא goes to the trouble of buying land with the tree's value. If the principal could be used up anyway, that would be pointless. The lender could just cut the tree for wood and keep it. So the ברייתא must be in a case where the land is kept for good.

phrases.english: So too it makes sense,
for if you would think
it is a time when יובל is in effect
and we do use up the principal,
let him chop it into firewood and take it!
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the lender holding the tree as a pledge, and 'it' is the dried-up tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in Step 19 with logic.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא is about a time when יובל is not in effect.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The logic of the ברייתא itself: buying land would be pointless if the principal could be used up.

steps.title: Even with יובל, the principal is not always used up
steps.stepSummary: The support is pushed away. Even when יובל is in effect, buying land can make sense, because the land may come back to the borrower before יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is the reason, it is not difficult. Sometimes the years of the pledge end before יובל. Or the borrower gets money and redeems the field four or five years before יובל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the support from Step 20. There are good reasons to buy land even in a time when יובל is in effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 assumed that with יובל, the principal is always lost, so buying land would be pointless. But the pledge may end before יובל, or the borrower may pay back early. In those cases the land still holds its value, so buying land is not pointless at all.

keyTerms.meaning: if that is the reason, it is not difficult
a field given to a lender as a pledge, which he uses for a set time

phrases.english: If it is because of this – it is not difficult:
sometimes the years of the pledge end
before יובל.
Or else, money comes to him
and he redeems it
four or five years before יובל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the logical support brought in Step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the support in Step 20, not the answer in Step 19 itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 20 assumed that when יובל is in effect, the principal is always used up. In fact the land may return to the borrower, or he may pay back, before יובל.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about the dried tree can be explained by רב: either it is a time without יובל, or, even with יובל, the principal is often not lost.

steps.title: רבי נתן on a rented boat that sank halfway
steps.stepSummary: A new topic begins. A ברייתא brings רבי נתן's ruling: if the boat sinks halfway, money already paid is not returned, and money not yet paid is not owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if someone rents a boat and it sinks halfway through the trip, רבי נתן says: if he already paid, he does not get it back, and if he did not pay, he does not have to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a brand-new topic with a ברייתא about a rented boat that sank in the middle of the trip.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן rules that whatever has already happened with the money stays as it is. Paid money stays with the boat owner, and unpaid money stays with the renter. The next steps will try to figure out what exact case makes this ruling make sense.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who rents the boat
and it sank halfway through the trip,
רבי נתן says:
If he paid – he does not take it back,
and if he did not pay – he does not pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the יובל discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a rented boat sinks halfway, paid rent is not returned and unpaid rent is not owed.

steps.title: What case? A specific boat with any wine does not fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רבי נתן means. It tries 'this boat, any wine,' but then the renter should get his money back.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it was 'this boat' and 'any wine,' then if he paid, why does he not get it back? He can say: give me a boat, and I will bring wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks exactly what deal רבי נתן is talking about. It tests a first guess and shows it does not fit the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner promised a specific boat and the renter did not name specific wine, the renter still has wine to ship. The owner can no longer give the boat he promised. So the renter should be able to demand his money back, which goes against 'he does not take it back.'

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? how exactly does this work?

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say it is with this boat and any wine,
if he paid, why does he not take it back?
Let him say to him: give me a boat,
since I am bringing wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא בִּסְפִינָה זוֹ וְיַיִן סְתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what exact case lies behind the ruling in Step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exact rental deal makes רבי נתן's ruling make sense.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first guess: a specific boat with general wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The renter still has wine and the owner cannot supply the promised boat, so the renter should get his money back.

steps.title: Any boat with specific wine does not fit either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the opposite case, 'any boat, this wine.' But then the renter should have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is 'any boat' and 'this wine.' But then, if he did not pay, why does he not have to pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the opposite guess and shows that it runs into the other half of רבי נתן's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner promised just some boat and the renter's specific wine was lost, the owner could still supply another boat. It is the renter who has nothing left to ship. So the renter should owe the rent, which goes against 'he does not pay.'

phrases.english: Rather, it is with any boat and this wine,

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא נָתַן אַמַּאי לֹא יִתֵּן?
phrases.english: if he did not pay, why does he not pay?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first guess failed, tries the opposite case and finds a problem with it too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second guess: a general boat with specific wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner can still supply a boat, and the loss is on the renter's side, so the renter should owe the rent.
steps.confusionAlert: Each guess clashes with a different half of רבי נתן's ruling. The first guess goes against 'he does not take it back,' and the second goes against 'he does not pay.'
